After Rollbar's Sept 2023 breach notice, a user noted that every project by default has a standing token with read privileges that never expires and is not opt-in, calling it "ridiculous."

A user found the breach notice wording concerning, saying "including" suggests the breach could be wider. They wanted an explicit statement that GitHub credentials for source code integration were not compromised. The notice listed usernames, emails, account names, project/environment names, project access tokens and service link configuration.

After Rollbar said third-party integration credentials are stored encrypted with a key kept outside the database, a user asked for more detail on the type of encryption, to be reassured the credentials could not be brute forced if the attacker obtained them.

Users criticized Rollbar for copying project access tokens to its data warehouse in recoverable plain text. They argued the keys should be encrypted or hashed with an application salt not stored in the database. That would protect against breaches via non-production datasources or even direct production DB access.
Rollbar's entire customer base received several test emails from internal testing ("Rollbar Exceptions from Keith"), apparently caused by email aliasing.

A commenter said Rollbar's setup seemed badly designed: an email sent to team@ automatically blasted a newsletter with that email's content, without any further input. They called it "ripe for accidental or deliberate misuse."
A Rollbar customer said the stray internal test emails "caused a certain amount of WTF this morning and head scratching."
